claim: Microbes have disproportionate impacts on the macroscopic world due to their ability to grow to large populations that collectively secrete massive amounts of secondary metabolites and alter their environment.
source: Microbes have disproportionate impacts on the macroscopic world. This is in part due to their ability to grow to large populations that collectively secrete massive amounts of secondary metabolites and alter their environment.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that frames the general importance of microbial secondary metabolism.

claim: The ability to make surfactants from glycerol varies inconsistently across the P. aeruginosa phylogenetic tree.
source: Here we investigated the biosurfactants that the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa makes and secretes to decrease the surface tension of surrounding liquid. Using a combination of genomics, metabolomics, transcriptomics, and mathematical modeling we show that the ability to make surfactants from glycerol varies inconsistently across the phylogenetic tree
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Lineages that lost the ability to make surfactants from glycerol are worse at reducing the oxidative stress of primary metabolism on glycerol.
source: instead, lineages that lost this ability are also worse at reducing the oxidative stress of primary metabolism on glycerol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding linking surfactant production to oxidative stress management.

claim: P. aeruginosa lineages produce surfactants if they can reduce the oxidative stress produced by primary metabolism and have excess resources beyond their primary needs.
source: Experiments with different carbon sources support a link with oxidative stress that explains the inconsistent distribution across the P. aeruginosa phylogeny and suggests a general principle: P. aeruginosa lineages produce surfactants if they can reduce the oxidative stress produced by primary metabolism and have excess resources, beyond their primary needs, to afford secondary metabolism.
evidence: This general principle is explicitly stated in the abstract as a conclusion from experiments with different carbon sources.

claim: Microorganisms cause infections.
source: Microorganisms touch practically every human activity, in harmful and beneficial ways: they cause infections (Morens et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morens et al., 2004.

claim: Microorganisms help humans digest food.
source: they cause infections (Morens et al., 2004) and help us digest food (Rowland et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rowland et al., 2018.

claim: Microorganisms can be used to make bioterrorism weapons.
source: make bioterrorism weapons (Henderson, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henderson, 1999.

claim: Microorganisms synthesize life-saving drugs.
source: and synthesize life-saving drugs (Demain and Fang, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Demain and Fang, 2000.

claim: Microorganisms contribute to climate change.
source: contribute to climate change (Bardgett et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bardgett et al., 2008.

claim: Microorganisms clean wastewater.
source: and clean our wastewater (Kartal et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kartal et al., 2010.

claim: The outsize impact of microbes on the macroscopic world comes from their ability to multiply to populations of billions that cooperate to transform chemicals in vast amounts.
source: The outsize impact of microbes on the macroscopic world that surrounds them comes from their ability to multiply to populations of billions that cooperate to transform chemicals in vast amounts.
evidence: This is a general statement about microbial population dynamics and their collective impact.

claim: Many chemicals that microbes release are secondary metabolites unessential to growth, development, and division.
source: Many of the chemicals that they release are compounds unessential to growth, development, and division: they are secondary metabolites.
evidence: This defines secondary metabolites as distinct from primary metabolism.

claim: It remains unclear why microbes invest in secondary metabolites.
source: But despite their importance, it remains unclear why microbes invest in secondary metabolites (Cavalier-Smith, 1992; Kell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cavalier-Smith, 1992 and Kell et al., 1995.

claim: Secondary metabolites enable cell-cell signaling.
source: Secondary metabolites enable collective traits like cell-cell signaling (Dufour and Rao, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dufour and Rao, 2011.

claim: Secondary metabolites enable microbial warfare.
source: microbial warfare (Demain and Fang, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Demain and Fang, 2000.

claim: Secondary metabolites enable pathogenesis.
source: pathogenesis (Nicas and Iglewski, 1985)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nicas and Iglewski, 1985.

claim: Secondary metabolites enable nutrient scavenging.
source: and nutrient scavenging (Albelda-Berenguer et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albelda-Berenguer et al., 2019.

claim: Collective traits enabled by secondary metabolites bring fitness advantages to a population.
source: These collective traits bring fitness advantages to a population (Maplestone et al., 1992)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maplestone et al., 1992.

claim: Secondary metabolites can bring a cost to the individual cell by diverting precursors, cofactors, and energy away from primary metabolism.
source: but by diverting precursors, cofactors, and energy away from primary metabolism they can also bring a cost to the individual cell (Yan et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yan et al., 2018.

claim: A secondary metabolite can be favored by natural selection if rB > C, where r is the relatedness among different genotypes, B is the benefit to the population, and C is the fitness cost to the cell.
source: A secondary metabolite that brings a fitness cost C to the cell and a benefit B to the population can be favored by natural selection if rB >C, where r is the relatedness among different genotypes across the population (West et al., 2006).
evidence: This is Hamilton's rule from social evolution theory, supported by citation to West et al., 2006.

claim: Population mixing and mutation are frequent in the microbial world.
source: But population mixing and mutation, which are frequent in a microbial world (Andersen et al., 2015; Andersen et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andersen et al., 2015 and 2018.

claim: Low relatedness in microbial populations limits the maximum cost allowed for secondary metabolites.
source: mean that microbial populations can have a low relatedness, and a low r limits the maximum cost allowed for secondary metabolites.
evidence: This is an inference from social evolution theory applied to microbial populations.

claim: Social evolution theory predicts that secondary pathways should have a low cost.
source: Social evolution theory therefore predicts that secondary pathways should have a low cost (Cavalier-Smith, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cavalier-Smith, 1992.

claim: Many secondary products need multiple enzymes for their biosynthesis.
source: But many secondary products need multiple enzymes for their biosynthesis (Osbourn, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Osbourn, 2010.

claim: Microorganisms have sophisticated molecular networks that can sense environmental stimuli and regulate the expression of secondary pathways to lower their cost.
source: Microorganisms have sophisticated molecular networks that can sense environmental stimuli and regulate the expression of secondary pathways to lower their cost (Brakhage, 2013; Bibb, 2005; Bayram et al., 2016; Lind et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Microbes can regulate the production of secondary metabolites depending on the type and quantity of nutrients provided, especially the carbon source.
source: Experiments in laboratory culture show, for example, that microbes can regulate the production of secondary metabolites depending on environmental conditions such as the type and quantity of the nutrients provided, especially the carbon source (Ruiz et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ruiz et al., 2010.

claim: Microbes can restrict secondary metabolite production to specific growth phases, typically the stationary phase.
source: that they can restrict production to specific growth phases, typically the stationary phase (Malik, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malik, 1980.

claim: Many secondary metabolites are controlled by quorum sensing.
source: and that many secondary metabolites are controlled by quorum sensing (Whiteley et al., 1999), a type of cell-cell communication that regulates genes in a density-dependent way.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Whiteley et al., 1999.

claim: P. aeruginosa secretes biosurfactants to decrease the surface tension of the surrounding liquid.
source: Here we investigate the evolution and regulation of biosurfactants that the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa secretes to decrease the surface tension of the surrounding liquid (Abdel-Mawgoud et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Abdel-Mawgoud et al., 2010.

claim: P. aeruginosa biosurfactants enable swarming.
source: These biosurfactants are secondary metabolites, and they enable spectacular collective behaviors like swarming (Tremblay et al., 2007; Deforet, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tremblay et al., 2007 and Deforet, 2022.

claim: P. aeruginosa biosurfactants enable climbing over walls.
source: climbing over walls (Yang et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2021.

claim: P. aeruginosa biosurfactants enable killing microbial competitors.
source: killing microbial competitors (Sotirova et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sotirova et al., 2008.

claim: P. aeruginosa biosurfactants enable breaching the epithelial barriers of a host.
source: and breaching the epithelial barriers of a host (Zulianello et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zulianello et al., 2006.

claim: A P. aeruginosa cell produces 20% or more of its dry weight in biosurfactants.
source: But a P. aeruginosa cell produces 20% or more of its dry weight in biosurfactants (Guerra-Santos et al., 1984), which is potentially a huge cost (Xavier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guerra-Santos et al., 1984 and Xavier et al., 2011.

claim: The RhlA enzyme catalyzes the first step in the biosynthesis of rhamnolipid surfactants by taking β-hydroxyacyl-ACP and producing HAAs.
source: The first step in the biosynthesis of rhamnolipid surfactants is catalyzed by the RhlA enzyme, which takes a metabolic intermediate from fatty acid synthesis, β-hydroxyacyl-acyl carrier protein (β-hydroxyacyl-ACP), and produces 3-(3-hydroxyalkanoyloxy) alkanoic acids (HAAs) (Zhu and Rock, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhu and Rock, 2008.

claim: The RhlB and RhlC enzymes each add one unit of rhamnose to the HAAs to produce mono-rhamnolipids and di-rhamnolipids.
source: The RhlB and RhlC enzymes each add one unit of rhamnose to the HAAs to produce mono-rhamnolipids and di-rhamnolipids (Chong and Li, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chong and Li, 2017.

claim: The expression of the rhlAB operon is regulated by a network that includes at least three quorum sensing signals.
source: The expression of the rhlAB operon is regulated by a network that includes at least three quorum sensing signals (Mukherjee et al., 2018; Latifi et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mukherjee et al., 2018 and Latifi et al., 1996.

claim: The expression of the rhlAB operon is conditional to the nutrients in the media, requiring a high carbon-to-nitrogen or carbon-to-iron ratio.
source: and is conditional to the nutrients in the media, requiring a high carbon-to-nitrogen or carbon-to-iron ratio (Xavier et al., 2011; Boyle et al., 2015; Mellbye and Schuster, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xavier et al., 2011, Boyle et al., 2015, and Mellbye and Schuster, 2014.

claim: Metabolic prudence delays the expression of secondary biosynthetic genes to times when the population is large enough and the individual cell has sufficient carbon source.
source: This regulatory strategy—called metabolic prudence—delays the expression of the secondary biosynthetic genes to times when the population is large enough, but also checks if the individual cell has sufficient carbon source to make the product at low or no cost to its fitness (Xavier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xavier et al., 2011.

claim: Metabolic prudence regulates the expression of other secondary metabolites in P. aeruginosa besides surfactants.
source: Metabolic prudence regulates the expression of other secondary metabolites in P. aeruginosa besides surfactants (Mellbye and Schuster, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mellbye and Schuster, 2014.

claim: Metabolic prudence may provide a general evolutionary explanation for secondary metabolites in other microbes.
source: and may provide a general evolutionary explanation for secondary metabolites in other microbes as well (Bruger and Waters, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bruger and Waters, 2015.

claim: Metabolic prudence lowers the C/B ratio and stabilizes biosurfactant synthesis by preventing cheaters from increasing in frequency.
source: Compared to the non-regulated constitutive production, metabolic prudence lowers the C/B ratio and stabilizes biosurfactant synthesis—even when r is low—by preventing cheaters from increasing in frequency (de Vargas Roditi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Vargas Roditi et al., 2013.

claim: Surfactant production varies widely among P. aeruginosa strains, even when they are closely related.
source: But this evolutionary explanation alone cannot explain why the surfactant production varies widely among strains, even when they are closely related (Müller et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Müller et al., 2011.

claim: The genes rhlA, rhlB, and rhlC are highly conserved in P. aeruginosa.
source: and even though the genes encoding the secondary pathway—rhlA, rhlB, and rhlC—are highly conserved (Germer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Germer et al., 2020.

claim: Glycerol is a relevant nutrient for P. aeruginosa infection.
source: Here we investigate surfactant secretion among diverse P. aeruginosa strains that we isolated from infected patients. We start by focusing on the role of glycerol as a carbon source, a relevant nutrient for P. aeruginosa infection (Scoffield and Silo-Suh, 2016; Abdel-Mawgoud et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Scoffield and Silo-Suh, 2016 and Abdel-Mawgoud et al., 2014.

claim: Glycerol puts a substantial strain on Pseudomonas primary metabolism.
source: that puts a substantial strain on Pseudomonas primary metabolism (Poblete-Castro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Poblete-Castro et al., 2020.

claim: The lineages that lost their ability to make surfactants tend to grow slower compared to lineages that can make surfactants.
source: Then, we investigate other carbon sources to search for a general explanation: we show that the lineages that lost their ability to make the surfactants tend to grow not less but slower compared to lineages that can make surfactants.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The inability to reduce oxidative stress produced by primary metabolism is linked with the lack of surfactant secretion.
source: Using metabolomics and mathematical modeling, we link the inability to reduce oxidative stress produced by primary metabolism with the lack of surfactant secretion.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study using metabolomics and modeling.

claim: The panel of 31 P. aeruginosa strains includes 28 isolates from infected patients and 3 type strains (PAO1, PA14, and PA7).
source: We investigated the phenotypic variability among clinical isolates in a diverse panel of 31 P. aeruginosa strains, including 28 isolates from infected patients (Yan et al., 2017) and the 3 types of strains PAO1, PA14, and PA7, all of which have their genomes sequenced.
evidence: This describes the strain panel used in the study.

claim: The wild-type PA14 causes drop collapse indicating surfactant secretion.
source: As expected, the wild type caused drop collapse indicating surfactant secretion
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the drop collapse assay.

claim: The PA14 ΔrhlA mutant does not cause drop collapse, indicating loss of surfactants.
source: the ΔrhlA mutant did not, indicating loss of surfactants
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the drop collapse assay.

claim: The complementation of the ΔrhlA with the L-arabinose inducible PBADrhlAB restored the drop collapse only when L-arabinose was added.
source: and the complementation of the ΔrhlA with the L-arabinose inducible PBADrhlAB restored the drop collapse but only when L-arabinose was added, as expected (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the drop collapse assay shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Among the clinical isolates, 17 were strong producers, 8 were non-producers, and 6 were moderate producers of surfactants.
source: Among the clinical isolates, however, there was a wide variability of surfactant phenotypes. The strongest producers (n=17) showed phenotypes similar to the wild-type PA14, while non-producers (n=8) showed no surfactant secretion similar to the ΔrhlA mutant; moderate producers (n=6) showed a phenotype in between.
evidence: This describes the distribution of surfactant phenotypes among clinical isolates.

claim: There was no obvious relation between the body site infected in the patient and the surfactant phenotype.
source: There was no obvious relation between the body site infected in the patient and the surfactant phenotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no coherent distribution of surfactant phenotypes with the isolates' phylogeny.
source: There was also no coherent distribution with the isolates' phylogeny, which we built using the sequence variation in core genes, also supported by a poor correlation in Moran's I test of p=0.14.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and Moran's I test.

claim: Ancestral reconstruction supports that the ability to make surfactants from glycerol was present in the common ancestor of all strains.
source: Ancestral reconstruction of the surfactant secretion trait supports that the ability to make surfactants from glycerol was present in the common ancestor of all strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The genes rhlA, rhlB, and rhlC were present in all 31 isolates, and their sequence was 100% conserved.
source: Importantly, the genes rhlA, rhlB, and rhlC, the genes encoding the secondary biosynthesis pathway, were present in all 31 isolates, and their sequence was 100% conserved.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the strains.

claim: The absence of surfactant secretion was not due to a loss of the biosynthetic pathway.
source: This indicates that the absence of surfactant secretion was not due to a loss of the biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that rhlA, rhlB, and rhlC are conserved in all strains.

claim: Some lineages may have lost their ability to rewire their regulatory network to overcome specific selective pressures during their evolution.
source: Instead, we hypothesized that the phenotypic variation was due to the life histories of the strains: some lineages may have lost their ability to rewire their regulatory network to overcome the specific selective pressures that they had faced during their evolution.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the phenotypic variation.

claim: Surfactant producers have faster primary metabolisms in glycerol minimal medium.
source: To search for a general explanation, we conducted analyses that showed producers have faster primary metabolisms in the same media of drop collapse assay.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analyses.

claim: The maxima that the population densities reached showed no obvious difference between producers and non-producers.
source: The maxima that the population densities reached showed no obvious difference in producers vs non-producers, but the cultures did vary widely in the shape of their lag phase and the exponential phase (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the growth curve data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The slope of the exponential growth phase was steeper in producers.
source: Instead, the slope of the exponential growth phase was steeper in producers.
evidence: This is an observation from the growth curve analysis.

claim: Non-negative matrix factorization showed that producers had higher weights for base 1, which agrees with a faster growth rate in the exponential phase.
source: This was also shown using non-negative matrix factorization (Lee and Seung, 1999), which could decompose each growth curve as a weighted sum of three basis functions (i.e. features). This analysis showed that—although the growth curves of the producers (orange lines; including mild and strong producers) and non-producers (blue lines) largely overlapped (Figure 2A)—producers had higher weights for base 1, which agrees with a faster growth rate in the exponential phase (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on non-negative matrix factorization analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Random forest classification revealed that the top two features associated with surfactant production were the maximum and the average specific growth rates in phase I.
source: Random forest classification revealed that the top two features associated with surfactant production were the maximum and the average specific growth rates in phase I, the exponential growth phase (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on random forest analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Features of phase III, such as the starting value of OD600 in phase III which represents the final biomass produced, were among the least significant.
source: Features of phase III (the decay phase), such as the starting value of OD600 in phase III which represents the final biomass produced by different strains in phase II, were among the least significant.
evidence: This is based on random forest analysis.

claim: The ability to make surfactants is associated with the speed of the exponential phases and an efficient primary metabolism on glycerol.
source: These analyses indicate that the ability to make surfactants, which typically peak when growth slows down from exponential (Latifi et al., 1996; Boyle et al., 2015; Mellbye and Schuster, 2014), is associated with the speed of the exponential phases, and hence, an efficient primary metabolism on glycerol.
evidence: This is an inference from the growth curve analyses, supported by citations.

claim: Non-producer lineages had particular life histories that are selected for specific metabolic adaptations that impacted their ability to grow on glycerol as a sole carbon source.
source: This suggests that the non-producer lineages had particular life histories that are selected for specific metabolic adaptations, and that those adaptations had the collateral damage of impacting their ability to grow on glycerol as a sole carbon source.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the growth curve analyses.

claim: LC-MS revealed 67 metabolites whose identities are known and whose abundances varied significantly across the tested strains.
source: Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)revealed 67 metabolites whose identities are known, and their abundances varied significantly across the tested strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS metabolomics data.

claim: Hierarchical clustering and PCA showed a reasonable separation between producers and non-producers based on metabolome data.
source: Hierarchical clustering and PCA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B) showed a reasonable separation between producers and non-producers.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering and PCA of metabolomics data.

claim: OPLS-DA confirmed that there is a significant association between the broad metabolome and surfactant secretion (R2=0.82, Q2=0.66, p-value = 5e−4).
source: Fitting the data using the orthogonal projections to latent structures-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) (Cloarec et al., 2005) confirmed that there is a significant association between the broad metabolome and surfactant secretion (Figure 3A, R2=0.82, Q2=0.66, p-value = 5e−4).
evidence: This is based on OPLS-DA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The most perturbed pathways in non-producers were the TCA cycle and amino acid metabolism.
source: The most perturbed pathways were the TCA cycle and amino acid metabolism (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis using FELLA, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Three out of six metabolites in the TCA cycle—fumarate, succinate, and citrate—were significantly changed between producers and non-producers.
source: Three out of six metabolites in the TCA cycle—fumarate, succinate, and citrate—were significantly changed: fumarate and malate had positive loadings, which indicated higher levels in producers. Citrate, succinate, and to a lesser extent cis-aconitate and alpha-ketoglutarate had negative loadings, which indicated higher levels in non-producers (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on OPLS-DA loadings shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pyruvate remained relatively constant across all the strains.
source: Pyruvate remained relatively constant across all the strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), implying that the differential responses in the TCA cycle were independent from the changes in its upstream central carbon metabolism.
evidence: This is based on metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The TCA cycle harbors five enzymes with Fe-S clusters: aconitase A, aconitase B, succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), fumarase A, and fumarase B.
source: First, the major differences include TCA intermediates (Figure 3B). The TCA cycle harbors five enzymes with Fe-S clusters, aconitase A, aconitase B, succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), fumarase A, and fumarase B (Py and Barras, 2010), which make them especially vulnerable to oxidative stress (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Py and Barras, 2010.

claim: Fe-S cluster-containing enzymes are especially vulnerable to oxidative stress.
source: which make them especially vulnerable to oxidative stress (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is general knowledge about Fe-S clusters.

claim: If non-producers are less successful at removing oxidative stress from growth in glycerol, then the stress accumulated could reduce flux through the TCA cycle, which would slow down growth.
source: If non-producers are less successful at removing the oxidative stress from growth in glycerol, then the stress accumulated could reduce flux through the TCA cycle, which would slow down growth.
evidence: This is a theoretical argument linking oxidative stress to TCA cycle flux and growth.

claim: The accumulation of succinate and depletion of fumarate in non-producers could be due to a reduced activity of SDH under oxidative stress.
source: The accumulation of succinate and depletion of fumarate in non-producers could be due to a reduced activity of SDH under oxidative stress: SDH is a membrane-bound dehydrogenase linked to the respiratory chain—a major site of ROS production in the cell—and also a member of the TCA cycle that catalyzes the oxidation of succinate into fumarate (Hederstedt and Rutberg, 1981).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by a citation to Hederstedt and Rutberg, 1981.

claim: SDH contains [2Fe-2S], [3Fe-4S], and [4Fe-4S] clusters.
source: Since SDH contains [2Fe-2S], [3Fe-4S], and [4Fe-4S] clusters (Ayala-Castro et al., 2008), ROS that damages Fe-S clusters could decrease SDH activity in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ayala-Castro et al., 2008.

claim: ROS that damages Fe-S clusters could decrease SDH activity in vivo.
source: ROS that damages Fe-S clusters could decrease SDH activity in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the vulnerability of Fe-S clusters to ROS.

claim: Non-producers had intermediate metabolites in amino acid biosynthetic pathways which are substrates of Fe-S containing enzymes.
source: Second, we saw that non-producers also included intermediate metabolites in amino acid biosynthetic pathways which are also substrates of Fe-S containing enzymes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on metabolomics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The glutamate synthetase has a large chain (encoded by gltB) and a small chain (encoded by gltD), and both subunits contain Fe-S clusters.
source: For example, the glutamate synthetase has a large chain (encoded by gltB) and a small chain (encoded by gltD), and both subunits contain Fe-S clusters that catalyze the production of glutamate from oxoglutarate and glutamine (Curti et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Curti et al., 1996.

claim: Non-producers had slightly higher oxoglutarate and glutamine as well as lower glutamate than producers.
source: Non-producers had slightly higher oxoglutarate and glutamine as well as lower glutamate than producers.
evidence: This is based on metabolomics data.

claim: Rhamnolipids secretion occurred when C:N flux ratio >6.3 in the genome-scale model simulations.
source: The rhamnolipids are produced when carbon is in excess (Boyle et al., 2015; Mellbye and Schuster, 2014) and, in the simulations, rhamnolipids secretion occurred when C:N flux ratio >6.3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on genome-scale modeling simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maximum growth rate was maintained at an intermediate flux range of NADH, NADPH, and GSH in the genome-scale model.
source: For all three redox molecules, we found that the maximum growth rate was maintained at an intermediate flux range (redox homeostasis; Figure 4A–C, upper panels, white area).
evidence: This is based on genome-scale modeling simulations shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The growth rate decreased gradually as the flux of redox molecules changed in either direction away from the homeostatic interval.
source: The growth rate decreased gradually as the flux of redox molecules changed in either direction away from this homeostatic interval (gray shading).
evidence: This is based on genome-scale modeling simulations.

claim: Before growth starts slowing down due to an excess in redox species, there was an abrupt shutdown in the overflow on carbon into many central carbon metabolites and in the secretion of HAAs, mono- and di-rhamnolipids.
source: Importantly, before the growth starts slowing down due to an excess in redox species there was an abrupt shutdown in the overflow on carbon into many central carbon metabolites and—importantly— in the secretion of the HAAs, mono- and di-rhamnolipids that makeup the surfactants (Figure 4A–C, lower panels).
evidence: This is based on genome-scale modeling simulations shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: The shutdown of overflow reactions under excess of redox molecules mimics the metabolic state in the non-producer strains who lose metabolic plasticity to overflow metabolites without compromising growth.
source: The shutdown of overflow reactions under excess of redox molecules mimics the metabolic state in the non-producer strains who lose metabolic plasticity to overflow metabolites without compromising growth (Vemuri et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results, supported by a citation to Vemuri et al., 2006.

claim: Forcing secretion fluxes to zero in the model did not predict a growth benefit.
source: When we forced these secretion fluxes to zero—to simulate a ΔrhlA mutant—the simulation did not predict a growth benefit.
evidence: This is based on genome-scale modeling simulations.

claim: The ΔrhlA mutant has no growth benefit in glycerol media compared with wild type.
source: This result agrees with data showing that the ΔrhlA mutant has no growth benefit in glycerol media compared with wild type (van Ditmarsch and Xavier, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Ditmarsch and Xavier, 2011.

claim: All strains except for M1608 quenched the H2O2 signal over the first 18 hr.
source: All strains except for M1608, one of the non-producers, quenched the signal over the first 18 hr (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on H2O2 removal assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Non-producers removed less H2O2 than moderate producers and strong producers.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the non-producers (blue lines) removed less H2O2 than moderate producers (green lines) and strong producers (red lines).
evidence: This is based on H2O2 removal assay data.

claim: Mild and strong producers have significantly higher per-cell H2O2 removal rates than non-producers (p<0.001).
source: We observed a similar relative trend of H2O2 degradation between non-producers and producers (Figure 4F): a linear mixed-effect model quantified the difference that mild and strong producers have in per-cell H2O2 removal rates, which was in both cases significantly higher than in non-producers (p<0.001; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on H2O2 removal assay data and linear mixed-effect model analysis shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: No gene passed the significance threshold (p<0.05) after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing in the correlation between gene presence/absence and H2O2 removal rate per cell.
source: To identify the genes that would explain the varying tolerance to oxidative stresses, we performed a Spearman correlation between gene presence or absence and the time averaged H2O2 removal rate per cell. No gene passed the significance threshold (p<0.05) after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple hypothesis testing.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of genomic and phenotypic data.

claim: Oxidative stress tolerance may be a system-level phenotype that depends on the interactions among many genes in multiple pathways.
source: It is possible that oxidative stress tolerance is a system-level phenotype that depends on the interactions among many genes in multiple pathways.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the lack of single-gene associations.

claim: The phenotype of oxidative stress tolerance can be determined by a small number of, but different genes for different strains.
source: Alternatively, the phenotype can be determined by a small number of, but different genes for different strains.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the lack of single-gene associations.

claim: The strain M1608 lacks katE, a catalase that degrades H2O2.
source: For example, the worst strain in this assay, M1608, lacks katE (Supplementary file 1), a catalase that degrades H2O2 (Mulvey et al., 1988)
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and supported by a citation to Mulvey et al., 1988.

claim: The non-producer strain F5677 lacks the redox sensor soxR.
source: and another non-producer, F5677, lacks the redox sensor soxR (Hidalgo et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and supported by a citation to Hidalgo et al., 1998.

claim: A PCA of the gene expression profiles could not cluster the strains according to their phenotypes.
source: A PCA of the gene expression profiles could not cluster the strains according to their phenotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on PCA of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The genes in the biosynthesis of rhamnose (rmlA, rmlB, rmlC, rmlD), rhamnolipid biosynthesis (rhlA, rhlB, rhlC, rhlR, rhlI), and quorum sensing (lasA, lasB, lasI, pqsABCDEH) were significantly less expressed in the non-producers.
source: As expected, the genes in the biosynthesis of rhamnose (rmlA, rmlB, rmlC, rmlD), rhamnolipid biosynthesis (rhlA, rhlB, rhlC, rhlR, rhlI), and quorum sensing (lasA, lasB, lasI, pqsABCDEH) were significantly less expressed in the non-producers (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In vitro data shows that the expression of genes including lasI, lasR, rhlI, rhlR, pqsA, pqsR, in P. aeruginosa PAO1, can be significantly reduced by quorum sensing quencher and oxidative stress by exogenous H2O2.
source: Interestingly, in vitro data shows that the expression of genes from the above list, including lasI, lasR, rhlI, rhlR, pqsA, pqsR, in P. aeruginosa PAO1, can be significantly reduced by quorum sensing quencher and oxidative stress by exogenous H2O2 (Mohamed et al., 2020), supporting that the loss of the phenotype is linked to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mohamed et al., 2020.

claim: The zwf gene encoding glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) was expressed higher in non-producers.
source: More importantly, the zwf gene encoding glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) was expressed higher in non-producers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: G6PDH is a major source of NADPH that contributes to antioxidant defenses by reducing oxidized glutathione.
source: G6PDH, a major source of NADPH that contributes to antioxidant defenses by reducing oxidized glutathione, was expressed higher, supporting our hypothesis that non-producers experience higher oxidative stress.
evidence: This is general knowledge about G6PDH function.

claim: Strong producers were enriched in acarbose and validamycin biosynthesis (pau00525), phenazine biosynthesis (pau00405), polyketide sugar unit biosynthesis (pau00523), starch and sucrose metabolism (pau00500), and pentose and glucuronate interconversions (pau00040).
source: The RLQ analysis also revealed the top five pathways enriched specifically in each phenotype group: strong producers were enriched in acarbose and validamycin biosynthesis (pau00525), phenazine biosynthesis (pau00405), polyketide sugar unit biosynthesis (pau00523), starch and sucrose metabolism (pau00500), and pentose and glucuronate interconversions (pau00040) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on RLQ analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Non-producers were enriched in the biosynthesis of siderophore group nonribosomal peptides (pau01053), ascorbate and aldarate metabolism (pau00053), monobactam biosynthesis (pau00261), D-glutamine and D-glutamate metabolism (pau00471), and sulfur metabolism (pau00920).
source: By contrast, non-producers were enriched in the biosynthesis of siderophore group nonribosomal peptides (pau01053), ascorbate and aldarate metabolism (pau00053), monobactam biosynthesis (pau00261), D-glutamine and D-glutamate metabolism (pau00471), and sulfur metabolism (pau00920).
evidence: This is based on RLQ analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Inducing surfactant synthesis in an engineered strain of P. putida reduces production of the final electron acceptor CO2, suggesting that directing metabolic flux to surfactant secretion could serve as an alternative electron sink.
source: Previous work in an engineered strain of P. putida showed that inducing surfactant synthesis reduces production of the final electron acceptor CO2, suggesting that directing metabolic flux to surfactant secretion could indeed serve as an alternative electron sink (Tiso et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tiso et al., 2016.

claim: In both PA14::PrhlABgfp and PA14::PA1/04/03gfp, the start of the exponential phase was increasingly delayed as the concentration of H2O2 was larger.
source: In both PA14::PrhlABgfp and PA14::PA1/04/03gfp, the start of the exponential phase was increasingly delayed as the concentration of H2O2 was larger (Figure 6A and C)
evidence: This is based on growth and GFP expression data shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: Once the exponential growth started there was no difference in the growth rate under different H2O2 concentrations in PA14.
source: but once the exponential growth started there was no difference in the growth rate under different H2O2 concentrations (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on growth rate analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PA14 can restore normal operation of its primary metabolism after removal of the extrinsic stress.
source: This indicates that PA14 can restore normal operation of its primary metabolism after removal of the extrinsic stress.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that growth rate is unaffected once exponential growth starts.

claim: The ratio of the median PrhlAB expression relative to the median PA1/04/03 increased linearly with the H2O2 concentration.
source: We determined that the ratio of the median PrhlAB expression relative to the median PA1/04/03 increased linearly with the H2O2 concentration (Figure 6F, orange).
evidence: This is based on promoter activity analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Extrinsic redox stress can induce rhlAB expression via a growth-independent mechanism that likely involves transcriptional activators.
source: Since PA1/04/03 measures the growth dependence of promoter activity (e.g. changes in number of RNA polymerases and ribosomes), the increased ratio showed that extrinsic redox stress can induce rhlAB expression via a growth-independent mechanism that likely involves transcriptional activators.
evidence: This is an inference from the promoter activity analysis.

claim: In the absence of H2O2, the ΔrhlA strain still attempts to express rhlAB at a similar level as the wild type (p=0.3).
source: The gfp dynamics showed that in the absence of H2O2 the ΔrhlA strain still attempts to express rhlAB at a similar level as the wild type (p=0.3).
evidence: This is based on GFP expression data.

claim: The lack of surfactant biosynthesis had no detrimental impacts on the primary metabolism in the ΔrhlA mutant.
source: We observed no decrease in the growth rate with increasing H2O2 concentration (Figure 6E), which indicates that the lack of surfactant biosynthesis had no detrimental impacts on the primary metabolism.
evidence: This is based on growth rate analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: H2O2 increased the expression of the rhlAB promoter relative to the constitutive promoter in the ΔrhlA mutant.
source: Similar to the PA14 wild-type strain, H2O2 increased the expression of the rhlAB promoter relative to the constitutive promoter in the ΔrhlA mutant (Figure 6F, blue)
evidence: This is based on promoter activity analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The baseline promoter activity increased significantly in the ΔrhlA mutant compared to the wild type (1.14×, p<0.01).
source: but the baseline promoter activity increased significantly compared to the wild type (1.14×, p<0.01).
evidence: This is based on promoter activity analysis.

claim: The genes for surfactant biosynthesis can be induced by extrinsic redox stress, and the induction is stronger if surfactant synthesis fails to start.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the genes for surfactant biosynthesis can be induced by extrinsic redox stress, and that the induction is stronger if surfactant synthesis fails to start.
evidence: This is an inference from the promoter activity experiments.

claim: D-glucose was the best carbon source for growth among the 190 carbon sources tested in BIOLOG arrays.
source: The data showed that D-glucose (also known as dextrose) was the best carbon source for growth.
evidence: This is based on BIOLOG phenotype microarray data.

claim: 40 carbon sources (including L-glucose) did not support growth of any of the strains (OD600 <0.05).
source: Also, we saw 40 carbon sources (including the non-metabolizable isomer of D-glucose, L-glucose) in which none of the strains could grow on (OD600 <0.05).
evidence: This is based on BIOLOG phenotype microarray data.

claim: The BIOLOG assay correctly determined 8/8 non-producers, which amounts to a 100% specificity rate.
source: The assay correctly determined 8/8 non-producers, which amount to a 100% specificity rate.
evidence: This is based on comparison of BIOLOG data with previous surfactant secretion scores.

claim: The BIOLOG assay failed to detect 10/23 producers, which amounts to a 43% sensitivity rate.
source: It failed to detect 10/23 producers, which amount to a 43% sensitivity rate.
evidence: This is based on comparison of BIOLOG data with previous surfactant secretion scores.

claim: The BIOLOG assay was mildly sensitive but highly specific: while it may miss some surfactant secretion cases, it is unlikely to overestimate the ability of a specific sugar to induce secretion.
source: Taken together, these results show that BIOLOG assay was mildly sensitive but highly specific: while it may miss some surfactant secretion cases, it is unlikely to overestimate the ability of a specific sugar to induce secretion.
evidence: This is an inference from the sensitivity and specificity analysis.

claim: D-glucose was the only carbon source (besides the positive controls) better than glycerol at inducing surfactant secretion according to the LASSO model.
source: The top three compounds were—as expected—the positive controls tween80, tween40, and tween20. This provided a sanity check that the model worked as intended. D-glucose came in fourth place: the only carbon source that the model deemed better than glycerol at favoring P. aeruginosa surfactant production.
evidence: This is based on LASSO model analysis of BIOLOG data.

claim: Glucose improved surfactant secretion overall, showing better secretion in seven strains relatively to the secretion in glycerol.
source: Consistent with our model, glucose improved surfactant secretion overall, showing better secretion seven strains relatively to the secretion we had seen in glycerol (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is based on experimental validation in glucose minimal medium shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Three strains that were non-producers in glycerol turned into producers in glucose.
source: this included three strains that were non-producers in glycerol but turned into producers in glucose.
evidence: This is based on experimental validation in glucose minimal medium.

claim: Four strains had worse surfactant scores in D-glucose than in glycerol.
source: Interestingly, the switch also went in the opposite direction: four strains had worse surfactant scores in D-glucose than in glycerol.
evidence: This is based on experimental validation in glucose minimal medium.

claim: None of the strains secreted surfactants in succinate.
source: Indeed, none of the strains secreted surfactants in succinate (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental validation in succinate minimal medium shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Phase I growth rate was unaffected by H2O2 in glucose, indicating that both PA14 wild type and ΔrhlA strains could still remove oxidative stress effectively.
source: Phase I growth rate was unaffected, indicating that both strains could still remove oxidative stress effectively (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on growth rate analysis in glucose with H2O2 shown in Figure 7D.

claim: D-glucose did not increase rhlAB expression with increasing H2O2 in either PA14 wild type or ΔrhlA strain.
source: But, contrasting with the results from glycerol, D-glucose did not increase rhlAB expression with increasing H2O2 in either strain (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on promoter activity analysis in glucose with H2O2 shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Carbon sources that place a lower burden on primary metabolism leave resources available to both deal with extrinsic oxidative stress and sustain surfactant production.
source: Taken together, these results support that carbon sources that place a lower burden on primary metabolism leave resources available to both deal with extrinsic oxidative stress and sustain surfactant production.
evidence: This is an inference from the glucose and H2O2 experiments.

claim: A strain can use its secondary metabolic pathways to produce surfactants if it can meet its primary requirements of energy production, biomass synthesis, and reduction of oxidative stress.
source: Here we investigated the evolution and regulation of surfactant secretion using diverse isolates of P. aeruginosa. Our results suggest a generalizable principle: that a strain can use its secondary metabolic pathways to produce surfactants if it can meet its primary requirements of energy production, biomass synthesis, and reduction of oxidative stress (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The lineages that retained their ability to make surfactants from glycerol were capable of reducing the oxidative stress created by primary metabolism and could overflow any excess carbon to the secondary metabolic pathway.
source: The lineages that retained their ability to make surfactants from glycerol were also those capable of reducing the oxidative stress created by primary metabolism and could overflow any excess carbon to the secondary metabolic pathway (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: Non-producing strains showed impaired abilities to reduce oxidative stress, a slower exponential growth in glycerol, and perturbed levels of TCA cycle metabolites consistent with oxidative damage.
source: Non-producing strains showed impaired abilities to reduce oxidative stress, a slower exponential growth in that carbon source (indicating a deficient primary metabolism), and perturbed levels of TCA cycle metabolites consistent with oxidative damage and accumulated intermediates of amino acid synthesis (also consistent with a slower primary metabolism).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: The burdens of oxidative stress may prevent non-producing strains from making surfactants as their resources are prioritized for primary metabolism.
source: Those burdens may be what prevented the strains from making surfactants as their resources were prioritized for primary metabolism (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: The OD600 at the end of exponential growth was not a good distinguisher for producers and non-producers, indicating that their final yield of biomass production was unaffected.
source: This was consistent with the observation the OD600 at the end of exponential growth was not a good distinguisher for producers and non-producers, indicating that their final yield of biomass production was unaffected, while their exponential growth was.
evidence: This is an observation from the growth curve analysis.

claim: All three genes of the secondary biosynthetic pathway (rhlA, rhlB, rhlC) were intact in non-producer strains.
source: Importantly, though, all three genes of the secondary biosynthetic pathway (rhlA, rhlB, rhlC) were intact
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Some non-producer strains could make surfactants in D-glucose.
source: and some of those strains could make surfactants in D-glucose.
evidence: This is based on experimental validation in glucose minimal medium.

claim: Absence of a selective pressure to produce surfactants from glycerol in the life histories of non-producer lineages could account for the loss of phenotype.
source: Absence of a selective pressure to produce surfactants from glycerol in the life histories of non-producer lineages could account for these results.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary history of non-producer lineages.

claim: The impaired ability to reduce oxidative stress in glycerol may be a maladaptive consequence of specific adaptations experienced by non-producer lineages.
source: But another explanation is that the impaired ability to reduce oxidative stress in glycerol is a maladaptive consequence of specific adaptations experienced by those lineages.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary history of non-producer lineages.

claim: P. aeruginosa decreases expression of key quorum-sensing genes (lasI, lasR, rhlI, rhlR, pqsA, and pqsR) in response to oxidative stress caused by exogenous H2O2.
source: Experiments in PAO1 and clinical isolates had shown previously that P. aeruginosa decreases expression of the key quorum-sensing genes (lasI, lasR, rhlI, rhlR, pqsA, and pqsR) in response to oxidative stress caused by exogenous H2O2 (Mohamed et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mohamed et al., 2020.

claim: Shutting down surfactant biosynthesis could be part of a broader response to reduce oxidative stress and save resources for primary metabolism.
source: Considering that quorum sensing regulates many genes (Whiteley et al., 1999), shutting down surfactant biosynthesis could be part of a broader response to reduce oxidative stress and save resources for primary metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of quorum sensing, supported by a citation to Whiteley et al., 1999.

claim: Adding extrinsic oxidative stress induced expression of rhlAB in glycerol for PA14.
source: For PA14, a strain capable of reducing the stress produced by glycerol metabolism, adding an extrinsic oxidative stress induced expression of rhlAB in glycerol, though not in glucose.
evidence: This is based on promoter activity experiments.

claim: ΔrhlA increased the baseline expression of rhlAB in both glycerol and glucose but did not impact the rate of rhlAB increase with H2O2.
source: ΔrhlA increased the baseline expression in both glycerol and glucose but did not impact the rate of rhlAB increase with H2O2, suggesting an intricate regulation.
evidence: This is based on promoter activity experiments.

claim: The lack of rhlA did not impact growth in glycerol or glucose compared to the wild type, even in the highest H2O2 concentrations tested.
source: Also, the lack of rhlA did not impact growth—in glycerol or glucose—compared to the wild type, even in the highest H2O2 concentrations tested.
evidence: This is based on growth experiments with H2O2.

claim: Shutting down rhamnolipid secretion in the flux-balance model did not impact the growth rate because the excess carbon could be alternatively secreted in other forms such as acetate.
source: This is consistent with our flux-balance modeling of Pseudomonas metabolism, where shutting down rhamnolipid secretion did not impact the growth rate because the excess carbon could be alternatively secreted in other forms such as acetate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on flux-balance modeling shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ΔrhlA isogenic mutant of PA14 has lower levels of fMet.
source: We did detect nuanced consequences of deleting surfactant biosynthesis in PA14: previous data shows that the ΔrhlA isogenic mutant of PA14 has lower levels of fMet (Boyle et al., 2017) which, interestingly, also happened in non-producer isolates analyzed here.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boyle et al., 2017.

claim: fMet plays a role in translation initiation and in the quality control mechanisms that degrade misfolded proteins.
source: fMet plays a role in translation initiation, and in the quality control mechanisms that degrade misfolded proteins (Piatkov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Piatkov et al., 2015.

claim: Bacillus subtilis lacking formyl-methionine transferase is more sensitive to H2O2 and defective in swarming.
source: Bacillus subtilis lacking formyl-methionine transferase—the enzyme attaching a formyl group to methionine loaded on tRNAfmet—is more sensitive to H2O2 and defective in swarming (Cai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2017.

claim: The ΔrhlA mutant had higher levels of gamma-glutamylcysteine, the immediate precursor of glutathione.
source: Also, the ΔrhlA mutant had higher levels of gamma-glutamylcysteine (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), the immediate precursor of glutathione.
evidence: This is based on metabolomics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Glutathione is a well-known antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.
source: Since glutathione is a well-known antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage (Ezraty et al., 2017), the result could indicate a mild oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ezraty et al., 2017.

claim: The finding that ΔrhlA expressed rhlAB at a higher level than the wild type suggests a futile attempt by this mutant to synthesize more surfactants.
source: The finding that ΔrhlA expressed rhlAB at a higher level than the wild type—in glycerol and in glucose—suggests a futile attempt by this mutant to synthesize more surfactants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the promoter activity data.

claim: The fatty acid biosynthesis pathway that provides precursors for surfactant biosynthesis regenerates NAD(P)+ from NAD(P)H.
source: The fatty acid biosynthesis pathway that provides precursors for surfactant biosynthesis regenerates NAD(P)+ from NAD(P)H.
evidence: This is general knowledge about fatty acid biosynthesis.

claim: ΔrhlA could perturb the fatty acid biosynthesis pathway causing minor increases in oxidative stress.
source: ΔrhlA could perturb this pathway causing minor increases in oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a speculation about the metabolic consequences of the ΔrhlA mutation.

claim: The model of metabolic prudence says that the microbial cell can lower the cost of a cooperative public good by delaying expression to times when it has excess carbon source.
source: Our analysis adds to the model of metabolic prudence, which provided a social evolutionary explanation for biosurfactant secretion. The model of metabolic prudence says that the microbial cell can lower the cost of a cooperative public good by delaying expression to times when it has excess carbon source (Xavier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xavier et al., 2011.

claim: The strain PA14 needs to regulate rhlAB expression to carefully split the flux of carbon between biomass production and rhamnolipid synthesis.
source: A detailed study suggested that the strain PA14, needs to regulate rhlAB expression to carefully split the flux of carbon between biomass production and rhamnolipid synthesis (Boyle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boyle et al., 2015.

claim: Heterotrophs like P. aeruginosa use organic compounds like glycerol, glucose, and succinate as carbon source for biomass and as an energy source.
source: Here, comparing diverse strains reminds us that heterotrophs like P. aeruginosa use organic compounds like glycerol, glucose, and succinate as carbon source for biomass, but also as an energy source.
evidence: This is general knowledge about heterotrophic metabolism.

claim: Energy from carbon sources fuels essential processes, including the reduction of oxidative stress, which ends up competing with secondary metabolism.
source: That energy fuels essential processes, including the reduction of oxidative stress, which ends up competing with secondary metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: Products of one microbial species can impact other species—cooperatively or competitively—potentially amplifying microbial functions in diverse communities such as the human microbiome.
source: Products of one microbial species can impact other species—cooperatively or competitively—potentially amplifying microbial functions in diverse communities such as the human microbiome (Xavier, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xavier, 2011.

claim: Natural selection will favor sophisticated regulation that conciliates the individual-level costs and the population-level benefits of secondary metabolism.
source: But their analysis suggests a general principle: natural selection will favor sophisticated regulation that conciliates the individual-level costs and the population-level benefits of secondary metabolism.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the study.
